channel.title: Signal Brief · Cloud & DevOps
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: Cloudflare lets sites offer a search API for AI agents with one toggle
item.description: Cloudflare has introduced Search for Agents, a dashboard toggle that creates an AI Search instance for a site, crawls and indexes its content, and exposes a search API from the site's own domain. The endpoint is advertised in page metadata so agents can discover it, and it supports the new HTTP QUERY method (RFC 10008) alongside plain GET requests. The feature is available to all customers, including free plans, and returns retrieved content in Markdown rather than a generated answer. Why it matters for tech: It gives site owners a standard way to make their content searchable by agents instead of being crawled page by page.

item.title: JetBrains' Mellum 2.1 coding model uses 45% fewer tokens by skipping the reasoning step
item.description: JetBrains has released Mellum2.1 Instruct, a non-reasoning coding model built for quick edits, tool calls and small tasks delegated by larger agents, answering without an explicit chain of thought. In JetBrains' agentic coding tests it generated an average of 5,600 tokens per task against 10,100 for its Thinking sibling, a 45% reduction, and it doubled its predecessor's SWE-bench Verified score from 20.2% to 40.4%. The model is open source under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face, including a GGUF version for running locally, and JetBrains is also releasing a multi-token prediction head it says speeds up generation by up to 1.8 times. Why it matters for tech: It trades reasoning depth for token economy on routine agent work, where the model is meant to handle quick edits and tool calls.

item.title: AWS opens a Bogotá Local Zone and doubles Lambda's timeout to 30 minutes
item.description: AWS opened a Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia, bringing low-latency compute closer to users there, and raised the maximum Lambda timeout for on-demand Event Functions to 30 minutes, double the previous 15-minute limit. The same weekly roundup notes GPU instances for Lambda Event Functions on Managed Instances and voice cloning in Amazon Polly. Why it matters for tech: The longer timeout removes a limit that shaped how teams split up agent and media work, and the Bogotá zone extends low-latency AWS infrastructure further into South America.

item.title: Agent Insights in Microsoft Foundry reaches general availability
item.description: Microsoft has made Agent Insights in Microsoft Foundry generally available, giving teams a way to observe agents running in production. The feature analyses an agent's recent traces with a model the team chooses, then groups recurring problems with their severity, the linked traces and a proposed next step. The same visibility now covers agents built outside Foundry with LangGraph, LangChain and CrewAI, by registering them through OpenTelemetry traces sent to Application Insights. Why it matters for tech: Agents fail in patterns across thousands of runs, so grouping those failures with evidence turns debugging from guesswork into a repeatable loop.

item.title: Microsoft Foundry now surfaces governance policy as agents are built
item.description: Microsoft has made governance policy guidance generally available in Microsoft Foundry, in both Foundry Canvas and the Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code. As developers build agents, the two experiences surface the policies that apply to the agent type, models, toolboxes and guardrails in use. The feature brings governance guidance into the tools where agents are built, so developers see the rules that apply to what they are building. Why it matters for tech: Policy checks that appear while an agent is being built catch rule-breaking choices early, when they are cheapest to fix.

item.title: A GitHub authentication bug signed users out of web sessions for two weeks
item.description: GitHub has resolved an incident in which users were repeatedly signed out of web sessions between November 5 and November 19, despite staying active. An authentication change had stopped web requests from renewing session activity and cookies, so sessions expired at their original time instead of being extended. GitHub says it deployed a fix on November 19 and is adding monitoring to catch drops in session renewal sooner. Why it matters for tech: Session handling sits underneath every web workflow, so a quiet renewal bug can sign people out without any visible error.

item.title: CloudWatch Omni now pulls in Azure telemetry
item.description: Amazon CloudWatch Omni can now collect Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network flow logs and Application Insights traces, AWS has announced. Teams running workloads on both clouds can now view Azure and AWS telemetry side by side in CloudWatch instead of maintaining separate monitoring tools. Setup connects a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to an AWS account and region, and the telemetry is available in all Azure public regions. Why it matters for tech: Multi-cloud teams usually stitch monitoring together by hand, and one console for both clouds shortens the path from an alert to the failing service.

item.title: Cloudflare WAF now blocks ruby2shell attacks on every plan
item.description: Cloudflare has added blocking rules to its web application firewall for ruby2shell, a critical heap overflow in Ruby's string case conversion disclosed on November 19 that Ruby rates as capable of remote code execution in some scenarios. The rules cover all customers, including the free plan, and a second rule covers a related integer overflow fixed in the same Ruby releases. Cloudflare stresses the firewall only buys time: the complete fix is upgrading to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10. Why it matters for tech: A firewall rule that ships to every customer at once gives teams breathing room to patch, but the flaw sits in the language runtime, so the upgrade is what actually closes it.

item.title: Five new nginx flaws can give unauthenticated attackers code execution
item.description: F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx on November 18, including five memory corruption flaws grouped under the name nginx2root that let an unauthenticated attacker crash a server or run code on it. The worst flaw, CVE-2026-123007, needs only HTTP/2 enabled and has been present since 2015, and Censys counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 on. The fixes are nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, and as of November 19 none of the five flaws was listed in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities catalogue. Why it matters for tech: nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so a remotely exploitable flaw in its HTTP/2 handling is a patch-now event for anyone running an exposed server.

item.title: Google makes sidecarless networking generally available on GKE
item.description: Google has made ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine generally available, offering a service mesh without sidecar proxies in every pod. Networking moves to shared per-node components and managed control plane services, with mutual TLS, authorisation policies and traffic telemetry built in. Google says the approach cuts resource use for layer 4 mesh features by up to ten times compared with sidecars and reduces pod restarts for proxy patches. Why it matters for tech: Removing sidecars takes the per-pod cost of running a service mesh off every workload, which makes mesh security and observability practical for clusters that could not afford the overhead.

item.title: Azure VMs can now recover across zones in public preview
item.description: Zone resilience for Azure VMs is now in public preview. It lets an eligible zonal virtual machine be recovered in another availability zone in the same region while keeping the same VM resource and configuration. Zone redundant storage managed disks replicate data synchronously across zones, so the recovered VM starts with its data intact. Why it matters for tech: A zone failure no longer has to mean rebuilding a VM by hand, which shortens recovery for services that run on single zonal machines.

item.title: AWS Lambda now runs GPU workloads for event driven functions
item.description: AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances, so teams can run machine learning inference, media processing, rendering and scientific computing as serverless functions. Functions are deployed as container images, Lambda handles provisioning, scaling and drivers, and the feature is aimed at inference rather than training. GPU functions support timeouts of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous work and up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage. Why it matters for tech: Serverless GPU support removes the cluster and driver work from small inference jobs, so teams can run a model as one step in an event driven workflow.

item.title: Microsoft announces Windows Server 2028 with hardened security by default
item.description: Microsoft has announced Windows Server 2028 at its Ignite 2026 conference, with a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline that cuts the work of securing a server from first boot. The release adds Trusted Launch for virtual machines, hybrid post quantum key exchange with ML-KEM, Intune management for servers and native NVMe storage enabled by default. It also adds AI accelerator support for running inference environments and open weight models on premises. Why it matters for tech: A server release that ships hardened and manages inference on premises matters to teams that must keep AI workloads inside their own data centres.

item.title: Azure HorizonDB leaves preview as Microsoft's cloud-native PostgreSQL
item.description: Microsoft has made Azure HorizonDB, its cloud-native PostgreSQL-compatible database, generally available in 13 regions. Microsoft says it delivers up to eight times faster transaction performance than self-managed PostgreSQL on its own benchmark, supports databases up to 128 TB, and fails over in under five seconds. A serverless version, Fabric HorizonDB, is in public preview and pauses compute after five minutes of inactivity. Why it matters for tech: Teams are asking one database to hold transactions, vectors, graphs and AI calls together, and HorizonDB is Microsoft's answer for PostgreSQL shops that want that in a managed service.

item.title: GitHub pull request merges timed out for hours before recovery
item.description: GitHub investigated elevated timeouts on pull request merges from 11:59 UTC on November 16, with timeout rates reaching about 4.75% against a baseline near 0.2%, and degraded performance in Actions workflows. Engineers reduced load on the affected systems and reported pull requests and Actions recovered, with the incident marked resolved at 16:26 UTC. GitHub said a detailed root cause analysis will follow. Why it matters for tech: Pull requests are the merge path for most software teams, so hours of timeouts stall releases and show how much daily development depends on one hosted service.

item.title: DuckDB's Quack protocol streams database results in column batches
item.description: DuckDB's Quack protocol, an HTTP-based client/server protocol, has reached its first production release in DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS. Instead of sending results row by row and repeating column names and types with every row, Quack streams results in batches of column data as DuckDB produces them, so clients can start working while a query is still running. The release adds a CONNECT statement for querying a remote server in SQL, command-line flags to start and connect to a server, and concurrent writes from multiple clients under multi-version concurrency control. Why it matters for tech: Database protocols built for row-by-row results waste bandwidth and memory on analytical workloads, so a columnar streaming protocol makes remote DuckDB practical for agents and apps that query data over HTTP.

item.title: DuckLake 1.1 turns data lake metadata into plain SQL tables
item.description: DuckLake 1.1, released in October alongside DuckDB 2.0.0, stores data lake metadata as ordinary SQL tables in a catalog database such as Postgres, MySQL, SQLite or DuckDB, instead of a separate metadata service. The open-source lakehouse works with DuckLake, Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake catalog formats, and its three layers are the DuckDB query engine, the catalog database and the storage itself. In the same month, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy announced the acquisition of DuckLabs on the company's third-quarter earnings call. Why it matters for tech: AI agents work through SQL, so a lakehouse that keeps its metadata as SQL tables fits agent-driven data work without a new query layer.

item.title: AWS Emulator gives agents a local copy of the cloud to test against
item.description: Amazon Web Services has released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS covering more than 200 services that developers select by changing one environment variable. According to the AWS announcement, the emulator was written entirely by agents, and a verification loop tests it against real AWS first, with a merge gate that has security agents review unimplemented features. Unimplemented operations return errors rather than fake successes, though the emulator does not simulate throttling, outages or per-region availability. Why it matters for tech: Agents need fast, realistic cloud environments to test their work in, and a local emulator with a checked fidelity loop is how AWS built one for its own agent teams.

item.title: Google Cloud brings agentic HPC to SC26
item.description: Google Cloud has set out its agentic high-performance computing plans for the SC26 supercomputing conference, centred on reusable agent skills that teach AI agents to build and run HPC workloads through Cluster Toolkit blueprints. The skills validate quotas and capacity before deploying a cluster, guide domain work such as fluid dynamics and life-science pipelines, and operate inside IAM and budget guardrails. The company is also showing AlphaEvolve on Cloud Batch for evolving code at scale, and new hardware including A5X instances on NVIDIA Vera Rubin and 8th generation TPUs. Why it matters for tech: Scientific teams are asking agents to run supercomputing workloads, so packaging HPC expertise into skills keeps those agents from misconfiguring expensive infrastructure.

item.title: AWS upgrades its AgentCore runtime for faster, cheaper agent sessions
item.description: Amazon Web Services has released a new version of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, the managed layer that runs AI agents in isolated Firecracker micro virtual machines. Sessions now start up to 15 times faster and scale to four times more compute, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of memory, while idle sessions scale to zero and reclaim memory within minutes. Agents can also mount storage such as an S3 bucket inside the session boundary, so data stays under the same controls as the compute. Why it matters for tech: Agents that run for hours need isolation that does not tax every minute of waiting, and this release ties billing and storage to how agents actually work.

item.title: Chainguard defends shipping PHP patches six hours before the agreed release time
item.description: Chainguard has defended its decision to publish patched PHP container images at 07:41 UTC on October 21, six hours and 19 minutes before the agreed 14:00 UTC coordinated release for the critical PHP2Shell flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Chief technology officer Matt Moore told KubeCon that attackers already had a head start, pointing to leaked vulnerability details, a mistakenly published proof-of-concept video, a honeypot exploitation attempt reported by Amazon on October 17, and attack traffic seen by Cloudflare. PHP said it found no working public exploit at release time, and CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26. Why it matters for tech: Coordinated disclosure only works when everyone holds the line, so an early release by one vendor forces the whole industry to rethink how embargoes are enforced.

item.title: AWS ships a local emulator that runs AWS APIs on your laptop
item.description: AWS Emulator is generally available: it runs on the laptop and answers AWS CLI, SDK and coding-agent calls over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs, with no additional service fee. It is built in Rust from the AWS API models, and an embedded mode runs inside test processes for the Rust SDK. AWS publishes per-service fidelity scores showing how closely the emulator matches real AWS, and an unimplemented operation returns an error instead of silently passing. Why it matters for tech: Developers and coding agents can test AWS calls without deploying, which shortens the loop for agent-built cloud code, though the emulator does not evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does.

item.title: NVIDIA hands OpenShell, its agent security runtime, to the CNCF
item.description: NVIDIA has donated OpenShell, its open-source runtime for securing and governing AI agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, where it joins as a Sandbox project. OpenShell runs an agent inside a sandbox and enforces policy on the files, networks, credentials and model endpoints the agent can reach, using Cedar as its policy language. The donation was announced at KubeCon North America, the project lists about 380 contributing organisations, and Red Hat, Docker and Canonical are among its core contributors. Why it matters for tech: As agents run longer tasks with real credentials, the controls around them become infrastructure, and neutral governance is meant to speed adoption across clouds and tools.

item.title: Ubuntu Core 26 enters public preview on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
item.description: Canonical has opened a public preview of Ubuntu Core 26 images for Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, bringing its immutable Ubuntu variant to public cloud marketplaces. Ubuntu Core builds systems from strictly confined snap packages and delivers updates as complete, auditable revisions with rollback, aiming to stop cloud virtual machines drifting from their original configuration. Canonical says the preview is for testing and feedback, and the images include cloud-specific kernel snaps and cloud guest agents packaged as snaps. Why it matters for tech: An immutable, drift-free operating system model on the three large clouds gives teams building appliances and managed services a smaller writable surface and a uniform image across providers.

item.title: Azure Front Door edge actions reach general availability
item.description: Microsoft has made Azure Front Door edge actions generally available, adding serverless compute at the edge of its content delivery network. Customers can run lightweight JavaScript functions while Front Door processes client requests and responses, for tasks such as modifying headers or routing decisions before traffic reaches an origin. Why it matters for tech: Running small functions at the network edge lets teams handle request shaping and routing close to users without adding a separate compute tier behind the front door.

item.title: Google launches TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max for AI inference and training
item.description: Google has launched two new TPU chips built on its TPU v8 architecture. TPU 8tx is aimed at confidential inference and offers up to two times lower latency than TPU 8t, while TPU 8i Max is aimed at training and fine-tuning and carries twice the compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, with two TPU 8i chips in one package. TPU 8tx supports clusters of up to 2,048 hosts with 24 terabits per second of cross-pod bandwidth. Why it matters for tech: New TPU options change the cost and speed trade-off for teams running large models on Google Cloud, and the confidential inference chip addresses regulated workloads that need hardware isolation.

item.title: AWS makes AgentCore Runtime V2 generally available in 10 regions
item.description: AWS has made AgentCore Runtime V2 generally available in 10 regions. Sessions now start small and page memory in on demand, and environments are snapshotted once and restored for each instance, holding P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB to 2 GB, against about 5.4 seconds rising to nearly 30 seconds on the original runtime. Why it matters for tech: Faster and steadier cold starts remove a common delay for agent workloads that spin up on demand, so teams can run agents without keeping idle capacity warm.

item.title: Perplexity's Teammates keep AI agents working between sessions
item.description: Perplexity has launched Teammates, a system that coordinates several AI agents which remember where past sessions left off and keep working without a new prompt. Shared project state lives in Git, with each project in its own repository and each agent working in a separate sandbox. Perplexity says fewer than 2% of agent submissions are rejected for being based on outdated state, with median submission latency under 1.7 seconds. Teammates is available first on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned. Why it matters for tech: Agents that keep working after a tab closes move AI tools from answering questions toward carrying out multi-step work on their own.

item.title: A decision framework for moving autonomous agents from Lambda to EKS
item.description: A senior QA engineer at Amazon describes an autonomous agent that reads test failures, files structured bug reports and catches regressions, running on AWS Lambda for one team at under $5 a month and about 200 invocations a month, saving 8 to 10 hours a week. Scaling the same agent to 50 teams changes the workload from stateless events to long-running, multi-tenant work with shared state and API contention, and the piece sets out when to move to EKS Auto Mode: when a workload needs persistent state, cross-tenant analysis, GPU bursts, namespace isolation and central rate limiting together. At 50 teams the EKS setup is put at roughly $200 to $250 a month in total. Why it matters for tech: The piece gives teams a concrete test for moving agents off serverless, which matters as agent workloads grow from one team to many.

item.title: Docusign turns AI coding tools into an engineering operating model
item.description: Docusign says all of its more than 1,100 engineers are now onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools, after early adoption stalled at 49% of engineers and an 18% productivity gain levelled off. The company credits a six-person Eng AI Champions team and about 75 AI Multipliers embedded in teams, with active usage reaching 93% within two months of the Multipliers starting, and lines of code updated per developer up about 52% from the starting point, though the article notes that volume alone does not prove faster delivery. Internal tools include Kody for coding, Chronicle for observability and DocuWiki for documentation, brought together in Krew, where teams build agents for recurring work under human review; no code enters the system unreviewed. Why it matters for tech: Docusign's numbers show the hard part of AI coding tools is not the rollout but the operating model around them, a lesson other engineering teams are now working through.

item.title: AWS makes Kiro bots generally available in Kiro Crew
item.description: Amazon Web Services has made Kiro bots generally available in Kiro Crew, its open-source multi-agent development environment. Each bot is a named, long-running agent with its own durable memory, kept in a notes file the developer can edit, and its own tools and permissions for one standing job such as triaging tickets or watching builds. A bot runs parallel worker sessions and can ask for more tools, but cannot take them without developer approval, and bots cannot delegate work to each other. Why it matters for tech: Giving each agent its own memory and a standing job shifts developers from carrying context between sessions to handing off whole processes.

item.title: Google hands gVisor and its agent stack to the CNCF
item.description: Google is donating gVisor, Agent Substrate and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, putting its AI agent infrastructure under neutral governance. gVisor, open sourced by Google in 2018, runs a lightweight kernel in user space to intercept system calls, adding isolation between containers and the host system, and is used by Anthropic and OpenAI to run untrusted code. Agent Substrate 1.0, now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine, lets agents pause when idle and resume without rebuilding their runtime, while OpenRL coordinates reinforcement learning training on a user’s own Kubernetes setup. Why it matters for tech: Sandboxing is becoming core infrastructure for agents that run untrusted code, and neutral ownership is Google’s bid to make its stack the default.

Cursor handles hosting, database provisioning and sign in, runs security checks for exposed credentials and secrets before publishing, and builds on Vercel for Platforms. The feature is available on all paid Cursor plans with cloud agents enabled, and targets internal business apps as well as personal projects. Why it matters for tech: Coding tools are closing the gap between generating an app and shipping it, which makes deployment skill less of a gate for new builders.
